activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million.
story:
The worksheet had been in Laura's back pocket since Friday, and by Sunday afternoon it was soft with salt and folded into quarters, the graph of carbon dioxide readings printed on the back like a seismograph of something enormous. She spread it on the flat top of the lifeguard station and weighted the corners with shells, because the wind off the water kept trying to take it. The quiz was first period Monday. Emmitt had missed the whole week with the flu and had texted her four times, the last message reading only, please, i can't fail another one, and she had promised to meet him at the beach where his little brothers were already shrieking in the shallows.

"You brought homework to the ocean," Roberto said, dropping his board in the sand beside her. "That's honestly grim."

"I brought Emmitt's homework to the ocean." She looked down the beach. Emmitt was walking toward them slowly, carrying his shoes, his brothers left with an aunt under a striped umbrella. "He has until tonight. I have until tonight."

The worksheet asked two things. First, explain how greenhouse gases trap heat; second, read the graph and find how much carbon dioxide had risen since measurements began. Emmitt sat down cross-legged in the sand and squinted at the paper as though it might blink first.

"Okay," Laura said. "Sunlight comes through the atmosphere and warms the ground, and the ground sends heat back up. Some gases let the sunlight through but catch the heat on its way out, so it sticks around longer than it should."

"Like a blanket," Emmitt said.

"Like a blanket," she admitted, "if I have to give you one sentence. It's more like a one-way door."

Roberto lay back on his board and closed his eyes. "I can't listen to this. It's Sunday."

"No one's asking you to prognosticate anything," Emmitt said. "She's the one doing you a favor."

Laura ignored them both and turned the paper over. The graph was a line climbing steadily across decades, and the question in the margin wanted the starting value, the number at the left edge, before anything else could be calculated. Emmitt traced the line with one sandy finger and said, "It starts around three hundred."

"You have to be exact," she said. "The question says measurements started at Mauna Loa. The station in Hawaii." She leaned closer, tilting the paper against the glare, and the tide charts in her head rearranged themselves. The first tick of data sat on March of 1958, and the value there was about 313 parts per million. She said it out loud so Emmitt would have it. "Three thirteen. March 1958. Write it in your own handwriting or it won't stick."

Emmitt wrote it on his arm with a pen because he hadn't brought anything, and the wind lifted a corner of the sheet and Laura slapped a shell down on it, and for a moment the three of them were all holding the paper at once, heads together, the sea dragging itself out in a long diminuendo behind them.

Then Roberto sat up. "You know Ms. Nielsen lives in that blue house," he said, pointing at the low fence behind the dunes. "The one with the wind chimes. She's the one who wrote that question."

"She wrote the question," Laura said.

"She graded the practice sheet Friday. Emmitt, your brother told my sister you missed the week. Laura, you got the start value wrong on the practice, she marked it in red." He said it without malice, which somehow made it worse. "You put three sixteen."

Laura stood up. The shells slid. She looked at the graph again, then at the dunes, then at the blue house with its chimes ringing in small nervous tones. She had read the axis the way she wanted to read it, grabbing the first bold gridline instead of the first point, and she had been confident, which was the problem with her, according to her mother, according to everyone.

She left Emmitt guarding the paper and walked up the sand, and Ms. Nielsen was in her yard taking sheets off tomato plants, an indigent scattering of plastic bags pinned everywhere against the wind. Laura asked, standing at the fence, whether the first reading was three thirteen. Ms. Nielsen said it was, about, March of 1958, and asked why she sounded surprised at her own right answer, and Laura said, "Because yesterday I had a different one." She thanked her and jogged back down the dune, where Emmitt was holding the worksheet above the reach of a wave that had come further in than any of them noticed.

"Three thirteen," she called. "I checked. It's staying three thirteen."

Emmitt wrote it a second time, on the other arm, in bigger letters, and the sea came in again and took the print of their footprints from the flat sand below the station, leaving the graph dry and the answer nowhere else but on him.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2000 study led by psychologist William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions.
story:
The playground behind the middle school had been their territory since sixth grade, and now, in the interregnum between graduation and whatever came next, Justin had claimed the picnic table under the oak for practice. He had an interview on Thursday at the garden center on Route 9, and he had a problem that showed up every time someone looked at him directly: his eyes went to their shoes.

"You looked at the ground four times," Haylee said, sitting across from him with a notebook. "I counted."

"Five," Sasha said from the swings, where she was pumping lazily with one leg tucked under her. "The fifth was when you said 'dependable.' You looked down right at the word dependable. That's the worst one to look down at."

Justin put his elbows on the table. "It's not that I'm lying. It's that when I have to think about the answer and the eye contact at the same time, one of them loses."

"So practice until they're automatic," Haylee said. She read off the notebook. "Tell me about a time you solved a problem."

"The swing chain on the old set jammed, and I oiled it with the stuff from Mr. Chukwu's garage." He held her gaze for the whole answer this time, and she nodded once, not smiling, like a proctor.

On Tuesday, Mr. Chukwu found them at the table while walking his dog along the riparian path that followed the creek behind the fence. He had been Justin's neighbor for eleven years, and he had watched Justin fail to look at him for most of those years. When Justin told him about the interview, Mr. Chukwu set the dog's leash on the bench and sat down.

"You will shake the hand of the manager," he said. "Handshake first, then the answers. Do it."

Justin gave him a handshake like something being returned to a library. Mr. Chukwu remonstrated gently, holding on: "Again. Firm. Not a contest, not wet paper." They tried four times. On the fourth, Mr. Chukwu said, "There. Now you believe yourself."

"It's just a handshake," Justin said.

"My grandfather would disagree with you," Mr. Chukwu said. "He read to me from his newspaper when I was your age. A 2000 study led by psychologist William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions." He picked up the leash. "Favorable impressions get boys hired. Practice on your friends."

Sasha abandoned the swing and demanded a handshake. Justin gave her the firm one, and she studied her own hand afterward as though it had been altered. "Do it again," she said, and they traded handshakes across the picnic table until Haylee protested that they looked like a pair of politicians at a ribbon cutting.

Justin spent Wednesday evening turning it over. Part of him liked the rule: firm handshake, favorable impression, done, a mechanism as reliable as the oiled swing chain. But another part of him, the part that had watched Haylee's pen move every time his eyes dropped, suspected that the study measured something he couldn't fake yet. His grandfather had a grip that had spent forty years on machine tools, and it was honest because the forty years were real. Justin's hands had moved lawns and jammed chains. A firm handshake from a person whose eyes fled the room might be a promise the rest of him couldn't keep. He couldn't decide whether the handshake was the fix or just the costume, and he decided, finally, that he didn't have to decide before Thursday.

The interview was in a small office with a window that looked out at rows of tomato seedlings. The manager, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, stood when he came in. Justin took her hand, firm, and held her eyes while he said, "Good morning. I'm Justin. Thank you for seeing me."

She returned the grip. "Good handshake. Most kids your age give me a fish."

"Tell me about yourself," she said, sitting, and opened his file.

He began with the swing chain, and he kept his eyes on hers, and when the answer ran long and he felt them start to slide toward the seedlings, he let them go, one second, and brought them back.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
The library smelled like radiator dust and old glue, and Jade had claimed the table by the window because its light made her feel more intelligent than she was. Two articles lay in front of her, both about the same question, whether debt shaped how nineteenth-century students chose careers. One had come from a thick journal with a blue cover; the other from a thin one she'd never heard of, published by what looked like a society with an impecunious budget and no marketing department. Her assignment was to compare them, critically, which was a word Mr. Becker had written on the board and then refused to define.

Bianca dropped into the chair across from her and spun one article around to look at it. "Easy," she said. "That one wins." She tapped the blue journal. "It says right here on the website, impact factor eleven something. The other one's like two. Use the good one, mention the bad one, done by dinner."

"That's not what comparing means," Jade said, but she said it without conviction, because an hour ago she had been doing exactly that. She had built her outline like a trophy ceremony: first place, second place, a paragraph of polite praise for the loser. It had felt efficient. It had also felt like something she'd copied off a rubric rather than thought.

"Then what is it?" Bianca asked, already peeling an orange in defiance of every sign on the wall.

Before Jade could answer, a memory surfaced, uninvited. Last spring, her history teacher had spent a whole lesson on historiography, how the same event looked different depending on who wrote about it and when, and Jade had thought it was a waste of a Tuesday. She'd wanted dates. Now she sat in the library with two articles on the same question and realized she was holding a miniature version of that lesson in her hands, and the teacher who gave it had retired in June. She would have to say thank you by email or not at all.

She pulled up the library database and typed the phrase from the journal's website. The first result was a definition, plain as a bus schedule. A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, was the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years. She read it twice. "It's about the journal," she said slowly, "not the article."

"So? Bigger number, still better."

"No, look." She turned the screen. "It's the average over everything the journal printed in two years. It tells you the journal gets cited. It doesn't tell you this article is good, or that the argument holds up. It doesn't even tell you the citations are flattering. People cite things to tear them apart." Bianca considered this while chewing.

Mr. Becker passed their table carrying a rolling cart of returns, paused at the word citations, and asked what they were fighting about. Jade explained the assignment, and the trap she'd nearly built into it, and he listened all the way through, which was rare for him. "So what will you do instead of ranking them?" he asked.

"I think I problematize the ranking," Jade said, trying the verb out and finding it fit her mouth better than expected. "The blue one has better data. The thin one asks the better question, the one nobody's asking, and its argument is messier but it admits what it can't know. If I just pick a winner I'd have to lie about one of them." Mr. Becker said nothing, which was how he said well done, and rolled the cart on toward the biography section.

Bianca had gone quiet, picking pith off her orange. "I did that," she said finally. "My whole draft. I picked the famous one and dumped on the other. I even wrote that its low citation count proved it." She looked at Jade's screen, then at the thin journal lying open to an article with careful footnotes and a section honestly titled Limitations. "Can I read that after you?"

"Take it now," Jade said, and Bianca took it to the far table and started over, which cost her the evening and, judging by her face, something else besides confidence in shortcuts.

Jade wrote until the window went from gold to grey. Her new outline didn't rank the articles; it put them in conversation, letting the thin journal's unanswered question sit beside the blue journal's unarguable tables, and it closed with a paragraph saying she could not yet tell whether the better question or the better evidence deserved the last word, and that she thought the honest thing was to leave both standing. Mr. Becker would probably mark it down for indecision. Or he might not. She saved the file, looked at the clock, and found she had missed the late bus.

"Walk home?" Bianca called from across the room, holding up the thin journal like a flag.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Herman and Chomsky's second filter is advertising: outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away.
story:
The printer in the media studies classroom jammed on the first page, as it did every Wednesday, and Amy hit the green button twice before bending to look through the plastic window at the crushed sheet inside. Rami was already at the layout table with his laptop open, and behind him the third-floor windows showed the parking lot going gold in the late afternoon. The November issue of the school paper went to the district print shop Friday at four, which gave them forty-one hours, and an hour ago the adviser's mailbox had delivered a problem.

Amy read the letter aloud once they had pried the paper free. Kestrel Hardware, three blocks from the school, was withdrawing its advertisement unless the paper retracted the article about wage violations at its garden centre, the one Jared had written after interviewing two former employees. "They give us two hundred a year," Rami said, not looking up. "That's the photography budget. All of it."

"Then we pull the story," Jared said. He said it fast, then slower, "I mean, do we?"

Mr. Das was in the supply closet hunting for toner, and Amy listened to him rattling cartridges while she turned the letter over. On the back, in ballpoint, the owner had scrawled a phone number and the words call me. She thought of her father watching the evening news, complaining one night that the channel seemed to love a certain developer and never said why. She had always assumed the anchors were just careless. The letter in her hand suggested something more deliberate, though she could not yet say what.

She went home and dug through her media studies folder. Mr. Das had assigned a chapter weeks ago, something by Herman and Chomsky, and she had read it half-asleep on the bus. Now she read it at the kitchen table while her mother steamed broccoli, and one section stopped her completely. She texted Rami: "come early tomorrow, before Jared."

Thursday morning the classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the cold radiators ticking. Amy had the chapter open on the desk between them. "They call it filters," she said. "Things that shape what counts as news before anyone decides anything on purpose." She tapped the page. "Herman and Chomsky's second filter is advertising. Outlets that live on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away."

Rami frowned at the sentence, then at the letter, which Amy had laid beside the book. "So we're a tiny version of that."

"Except we're a weird amalgam," Amy said. "Two hundred dollars from a hardware store and a school board that pays for paper. Half public, half begging." She laughed a little at herself, at the grandeur of comparing the Lakeside Ledger to a television network, and Rami laughed too, the way you laugh at something true and slightly bleak.

They called the owner from the classroom phone at lunch, with Mr. Das present but silent, unpacking his sandwich in the corner. The owner's voice came through the speaker, surprisingly mild. He did not shout. He said the article had hurt his business, that he had known the fathers of half these kids, that he had never asked for anything before. When Amy asked what specifically was untrue, there was a long pause, and then he said the employees had signed forms, and that the forms were a private matter. Jared, who had joined them by then, said quietly, "I have the forms. They're not private." The owner said he would think about it and hung up.

Jared spent the last period of the day re-reading his own article, hunting for errors the way you check a map after taking a wrong turn. He found one misspelled name and corrected it, which felt important and changed nothing. "The facts are the facts," he said. "The filters aren't about facts." Amy wrote that in her notebook, then underlined it, then felt unsure and stopped underlining things.

Mr. Das, wiping marker dust from his hands, told them only that the decision was theirs and that the print shop closed at four. He ate an apple with his feet on a chair, refusing, apparently on principle, to be consulted, though once he said, "The Ledger has survived worse than a hardware store," and would not elaborate, and Rami spent ten minutes trying to imagine what.

Amy stood at the window while the others argued budget numbers, watching the turbid brown of the creek behind the parking lot, swollen with last week's rain, carrying leaves toward the drain grate. She thought about her father's news channel again. Maybe the anchors were careless and maybe they weren't, and she had no way to know from her kitchen table, which bothered her more than the hardware store did. What she could know was this paper, this week, this choice. She turned around.

"We run it," she said. "With a box on page two explaining that an advertiser asked us to pull it and we didn't, and naming them, politely." Rami began recalculating the budget, cutting two photo pages, muttering that the creek in November probably photographed poorly anyway. Jared pulled up his article and set the headline one size larger, then sat back, enraptured by his own screen in a way Amy had never seen from him before. At 3:52 on Friday she carried the print-ready file down the hall on a flash drive, and outside the print shop door she could still hear Rami behind her, calling out that if they ever got rich, the photography budget was the first thing restored.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, both women's hearts are exposed, and a single blood vessel connects them, winding through their hands and hearts.
story:
John had agreed to write the essay only because Amine had promised to trade him a critique of the biology lab report in return, and now he sat at his grandmother's dining table with a library book propped against the sugar bowl, a printed reproduction of The Two Fridas beside it, and a page of notes that said nothing except "colour? composition?" in handwriting that got smaller toward the bottom, as though his hand already knew it was losing the argument.

The house was his grandmother's, technically, but his grandfather had claimed the back room decades ago and held it still: shelves of record albums, a card table with a permanent jigsaw on it, a window that looked onto the alley where someone's obstreperous dog announced every passing bicycle. John had come here to work because his own house was full of younger cousins on Sunday, and his grandfather had said, without looking up from the puzzle, "Sit, then. Mumble at the painting until it mumbles back."

He was tracing the composition with a pencil on scrap paper, copying the two seated women the way Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya had shown them in class, blocky shapes first, the direction of the arms, the storm pressing down from the top of the canvas. The sky was all bruised grey and ivory, and the ground below the women was pale, almost nothing, so that they seemed to float on a page rather than sit on an earth. He wrote "figures dominate, horizon high, emptiness below" and felt the small satisfaction of a term landing in the right place. Then he noticed, because his pencil had to go somewhere, that the two women were not merely holding hands.

He leaned closer to the reproduction. In one woman's lap lay a stripped, bleeding heart, and in the other's chest sat a smaller, whole one, and the line that ran between them was not a ribbon or a decorative sash. He sketched it: from the heart in the left woman's chest, down through her forearm, across into the other's fingers, up to her shoulder and into the second heart. One red line. His pencil followed it the whole way, and when he finished, his hand had drawn a single unbroken vessel passing through both their hands and both their hearts.

"Amine," he said, because Amine had arrived twenty minutes ago and was eating crackers and pretending to help. "Come look at this. Both of their hearts are exposed, and there's one blood vessel connecting them. It winds through their hands and their hearts. One line for the whole painting."

"So it's, like, the composition," Amine said, chewing. "The line literally holds them together."

"I don't know if it's composition or symbolism," John said. "That's the problem. Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya wants us to keep them separate, and the painting won't."

He tried anyway. Colour first: the European dress on the left, white and lacy, threaded with red at the sleeve where the vessel had been cut, and the Tehuana dress on the right in greens and blues and warm ochres, holding a small portrait of a man. Warm against cold, one bleeding, one not bleeding, or not bleeding much. Composition: mirrored poses, a shared bench, symmetry that the blood line broke, since the line dipped and sagged between their hands like something with weight. Symbolism: the storm, the exposed hearts, the scissors, the portrait held like an amulet. Every time he wrote a sentence under one heading, the evidence slid into another. The red of the vessel was colour, was structure, was meaning, and no category he owned could absolve him of choosing wrongly.

His grandfather drifted over with two glasses of lemonade and stood behind him for a long moment, saying nothing, which John understood as permission to keep going. "She painted herself twice," the old man said finally. "After something, I'd guess." He tapped the bleeding heart with one finger, not quite touching the page. "The one on the left is letting it out. The one on the right is holding it in. And the string says she can't choose." Then he went back to the puzzle, and John sat with that, because it was not analysis, it was something older than analysis, and he could not put it in the essay without pretending it was his own thought, and he could not leave it out without lying about how the painting had reached him.

By evening he had three paragraphs he half trusted and one he would have to cut. The last one argued that the connecting vessel was the real subject of the picture, that everything else, the sky, the dresses, the two faces, existed to give that line somewhere to travel, and he knew he could not prove it. He was honest in the margin about that: "The line carries the meaning, or the meaning carries the line; uncertain." Amine had gone home, the dog in the alley had finally quieted, and his grandmother was asleep in front of the television with the sound off, her consciousness somewhere John couldn't follow. He copied the essay onto clean paper, capped the pen, and looked one more time at the reproduction. Then he took his scrap sketch, the one with the vessel drawn through both figures, folded it in half, and put it in his pocket.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, published since 2002, scores 180 countries and counts concentration of media ownership as one pressure on press freedom.
story:
The argument started over the gravy boat, which Eli considered the most absurd possible origin for a war about the news. His father had read aloud a headline about the new bypass, the one that would run behind the school, and said the paper had it exactly right, that the bypass was a triumph of planning. Eli said he'd read the opposite that afternoon, in a story on his phone, and his father said, "Then your phone is wrong," in the voice he used when he meant the discussion was over.

It wasn't over. Eli's mother kept passing potatoes with the cautious neutrality of a border guard, but Eli had something he hadn't shown anyone yet, and it was burning a hole in his pocket the way only a folded printout can. He had cajoled Grace into helping him at lunch, mostly by promising to carry her lab reports for a month, and she had found the thing he needed faster than he would have admitted. She'd slid her laptop toward him in the library and said, "Look at this. The World Press Freedom Index. Reporters Without Borders publishes it. It's been around since 2002, and it scores 180 countries." She'd tapped the screen. "And guess what counts against a country's score. Concentration of media ownership. When a few companies own everything, that's one of the pressures they measure."

Eli had nodded like he'd known that all along. He hadn't. He'd spent the weekend in a slow, suspicious fog, ever since his father had come home from work on Friday unusually cheerful, humming, holding an envelope. Eli had seen the envelope again on Saturday, left open on the desk in the study: a letter from the paper that ran his father's monthly column, thanking him for his contribution and enclosing what it called an honorarium. His father was impecunious in the way of adjunct architects, always between commissions, and two hundred dollars for eight hundred words was not nothing. Eli understood that. He also understood that the envelope's letterhead had changed recently, that the paper had been bought, and that the new owner's name appeared in exactly one other place Eli knew of: a planning document about the bypass route.

All of that was why the gravy boat moment mattered. Eli set down his fork and said, "Dad, who owns the paper now?"

His father took a second too long. "A media group. Why?"

"Because the media group's owner also owns half the land the bypass goes through, and your column this month says the bypass is, quote, overdue and brave."

The kitchen went very quiet, the specific quiet of a refrigerator hum suddenly becoming audible. His mother put down the serving spoon. His father's face did three things at once, and Eli watched it try to settle on one of them. "That column," his father said slowly, "was my honest opinion."

"Was it your opinion before the honorarium or after?"

"Eli," his mother said, but softly, more warning than scolding.

His father pushed back his chair, not to leave, Eli could see, but to have something to do with his body. He went to the counter and stood there with his hands flat on it. "You think I'm bought for two hundred dollars?"

"I think you're bought for two hundred dollars and a compliment," Eli said. "The letter called your voice, quote, indispensable. That's not a fact, that's a cajole with a stamp on it."

To his surprise, his father laughed. It came out cracked and involuntary, and it changed something in the room. He came back and sat down and, instead of eating, picked up Eli's printout, the one Grace had helped him make, with the rankings and the bit about ownership concentration highlighted in yellow. He read it twice. "Since 2002," he muttered. "A hundred and eighty countries. They actually score this."

"That's the part that got me," Eli said. "It's not a feeling. Somebody counts it."

They were both quiet then. Eli realized, with an uncomfortable lurch, that he didn't actually know whether his father had changed his mind or merely his tactics, and that he couldn't know, probably ever, what his father would have written without the envelope. Maybe his father didn't know either. That was the part Grace had shrugged about in the library, the part Eli had carried home like a stone: the index could tell you who owned the papers, and it could tell you that it mattered, but it couldn't tell you what any one man believed on a Tuesday in a study with a check on the desk.

"So what do you want me to do," his father said, "send the money back?"

"I want you to write the next one whatever way you'd write it if they paid you in applause and bus tickets."

His father looked at the envelope on the counter, then at the yellow highlighter bleeding through the printout, then at his son. He picked up his fork and pointed it at the potatoes. "Pass those," he said. "And tomorrow you're coming with me to drop off the column. You can read it in the car."

Eli passed the potatoes. He'd read it in the car, all right, twice.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: An adjustable-rate mortgage's interest rate changes periodically with a market index, so its monthly payment can rise, unlike a fixed-rate mortgage's.
story:
The listing said "open house, 2 to 4," and Jayden had printed it out and folded it into quarters, the way his mother folded the bills she sorted at the kitchen table. He was the first one there. Mr. Moretti, who owned the building and lived one floor down, let him in with a ring of keys that sounded like a small toolbox. "You looking for yourself?" he asked, and Jayden said, "For my mom and me. She's at work. I'm doing the looking."

The apartment was smaller than the photos had made it seem, a trick of wide lenses that Jayden was beginning to understand was standard. One bedroom, a galley kitchen, a living room with a radiator that ticked even in June. Mr. Moretti named the rent, then named it again more slowly when Jayden took out his phone to type it. "First month, last month, and a security deposit," Mr. Moretti said. "That's standard. You get the deposit back when you move out, if the place is in shape." Jayden did the arithmetic in his head, multiplying by three, and felt the number land somewhere behind his ribs. His mother had saved for eleven months to get here, and the savings equaled almost exactly the entry fee for a unit that cost a third of her paycheck every month after that.

Tatiana arrived with Amanda, both of them clutching their own printouts, because Tatiana's father had declared that their family was done renting. "It's money that just leaves," Tatiana said, walking the perimeter of the living room. "My dad says rent is paying someone else's mortgage." Mr. Moretti, who was watering a sad plant on the sill as though he hadn't heard, said, "My mortgage, actually. That's the arrangement." He said it mildly, but Amanda caught Tatiana's eye, and there was a small silence in which everyone recalculated.

Tatiana had questions she'd written on her phone, and she put them to Mr. Moretti with the seriousness of a courtroom. How much was the down payment on a place like this building. What the mortgage would run. Whether it was true you could buy with five percent down. Mr. Moretti answered honestly, which Jayden respected, even when the answers were grim. The down payment was tens of thousands; the mortgage, monthly, was close to what Jayden's mother would earn in two weeks. "But you're building equity," Tatiana said. "It's not like rent." "It's not," Mr. Moretti agreed. "Though this year the payment went up on me."

Amanda watched Tatiana press her lips together, and understood, the way she understood things about Tatiana from the set of her shoulders, that this was the detail that would bother her all the way home. The building hadn't changed. The apartment hadn't changed. Mr. Moretti hadn't missed a payment or taken on new debt; he'd said so, unprompted, almost embarrassed. And yet the number he owed each month had climbed, and he was standing in his own hallway admitting it to two teenagers and a boy with a folded printout. Amanda thought about her own parents' fixed mortgage, the word fixed, how her father said it the way other men said locked in. She'd never once considered that a payment could move.

Jayden had been listening from the kitchen doorway, and now he asked the question he'd been turning over. "If nothing changed, why did it go up?" Mr. Moretti rubbed the back of his neck. "I've got an adjustable-rate," he said. "That's the whole story." Tatiana looked from him to Jayden and back. "Adjustable," she repeated. "As opposed to fixed." Jayden watched Mr. Moretti nod, and the mechanism assembled itself in his mind with a click he could almost hear: adjustable meant the rate moved when the market moved, fixed meant it didn't, and a payment tied to a moving rate could rise out of nowhere, without anything about the apartment or the borrower changing at all. He thought of the specious comfort in the phrase "building equity," how it could paper over a number that might not stay a number.

Earlier that week, Tatiana had accused him of hiding behind circumlocution, of talking around his real opinion instead of stating it, and it had stung because it was true. He had a habit of leaving himself exits. But standing in Mr. Moretti's kitchen, he found he could say a plain thing. "I came here to figure out whether renting makes us foolish," he said. "My mom thinks it does. My aunt says homeowners are the foolish ones right now. I wanted to see which one was right." He looked at the ticking radiator, the water stain shaped like a county on the ceiling. "I think the answer is that renting is what we can afford to be wrong about."

Tatiana considered that for longer than Amanda expected her to. Her father's certainty, which she had carried in like a coat, suddenly felt heavy and not entirely hers. "My dad would call that giving up," she said. "He'd say you're paying for someone else to abscond with your future." She paused, hearing her own circumlocution, and corrected herself plainly. "He'd say you're throwing money away." Jayden shook his head. "The money isn't thrown. It buys a roof with no surprises attached to it. Nothing here can jump on us." He didn't add what he was also thinking, that nothing here could be owned either, that his mother would turn sixty in apartments. He let the uncertainty sit in him without resolving it, because that was the honest shape of it.

Mr. Moretti took the application from the drawer and set it on the counter between them. "You want to fill it out, you fill it out," he said. "You want to take it to your mother first, that's fine too." Jayden picked it up and slid it into the folder with the printout, feeling the paper's slight weight, how little there was of it. Tatiana and Amanda were already at the door, arguing softly about down payments and what her father would say, their voices carrying down the stairwell. Jayden thanked Mr. Moretti, and the old man went back to watering the plant. In the hallway, Jayden stopped and texted his mother a photograph of the kitchen, the sink, the window with its ordinary light. Then he wrote, "Bring your checkbook Saturday. And ask your boss about overtime."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
Lauren had the keys in her fist before the instructor arrived, standing in the driveway between her mother's automatic and the family's old manual, a grey hatchback with a gearstick her father still called the brain of the car. The voucher in her other pocket was her grandmother's doing, munificent in a way that embarrassed her, twenty lessons paid in full on the understanding that Lauren would finally learn to drive. Sahar sat on the low wall by the mailbox, knees drawn up, watching the same two cars with open interest.

"Which one are you doing it in?" Sahar asked.

"The school's car. It's automatic. The man on the phone said it's easier, fewer things to fail on." Lauren turned the keys over. They belonged to the manual, which her father had promised would be hers next year if she proved careful. She had said yes to the automatic lessons without thinking, the way she said yes to most arrangements made on her behalf.

Karen had told her something at the bus stop two days earlier, in her flat, certain voice, the voice she used for facts she had looked up once and never doubted. "In the UK, if you pass your test in an automatic, you can only drive automatics. You'd have to pass a whole other test before you could drive a manual." Lauren had nodded and changed the subject to the seating plan for graduation, and only that night, lying awake, did the shape of the problem arrive. The licence she was about to spend her grandmother's money on would not cover the car parked four metres from her feet.

She had meant to check. Instead she had let it sit, the way an unresolved thing sits, neither accepted nor dismissed, and now the instructor's small hatchback pulled up at the curb and there was no more room for sitting.

He was a patient man named nothing she caught, and he drove the passenger seat like a place he lived. The first hour was mirrors, signals, the slow ballet of the driveway, backing out and pulling in while Ms. Johansson watered her roses next door and gave a small wave each time Lauren stalled the school car, which was impossible to stall, which was the entire seduction of it. On her sixth run to the curb, smooth as pouring tea, the instructor said, "You're a natural. Most learners fight the pedals. You're letting the car subsume the work." Lauren smiled and then did not, because the sentence had landed on the other problem, the one still in her pocket.

The instructor's viewpoint, if anyone had asked, was that the girl on her first lesson was watching her own hands too closely, and that whatever she was deciding was larger than a clutch. He had taught long enough to know that some learners chose the automatic licence for good reasons and spent years content, while others chose it and felt the limit like a low ceiling. He said none of this. He said, "Take us around the block," and Lauren did, and it was easy, and easiness was exactly the question.

Back in the driveway, engine off, she took out her phone and read the school's own terms straight off the website, holding the screen where Sahar could see it. "It's true. What Karen said. Automatic pass, automatic only. Manual needs its own test." Sahar leaned in, read it twice, and looked up at the grey hatchback, then at Lauren. In biology they had learned that a genus holds many species under one name, and Sahar thought of that now, the word "licence" pretending to be one thing when it was two. "So one licence is under the other," she said slowly. "Except it isn't. Not really. Not unless you pass the harder one."

Lauren walked to the manual and put her palm flat on the bonnet, warm from the afternoon. Twenty lessons, her grandmother's generosity, one easy path already half chosen, and beside it a smaller, harder door she had walked past every day of her life without opening. She did not decide then. She stood between the cars while Ms. Johansson's hose hissed against the roses, and after a while she turned and said, "Next week, ask them if they have a manual car."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
story:
The rain had been falling since four, sheeting the kitchen window so that the yard beyond looked like a painting left in the sun, colors running into each other. Sienna turned her learner's permit over on the table while her father dried his coffee mug and said, for the third time, that a road was only water and metal and you had to respect both. He distrusted driving schools the way he distrusted most institutions, a habit of mind she had inherited along with his stubborn chin. Ms. Korhonen, who had taught half the neighborhood to drive from the passenger seat of her ancient sedan, was waiting in the driveway with the engine running, and she believed in checklists the way Sienna's father believed in instinct.

"Mirrors, seat, seatbelt," Ms. Korhonen said as Sienna slid in, and Sienna repeated the sequence under her breath like a girl trying to codify everything her body did not yet know. The auxiliary brake pedal on the passenger side gleamed faintly, unused so far, and Sienna found its presence both comforting and faintly insulting, a net strung below a tightrope she had not yet stepped onto.

They drove the quiet streets first, past Jordyn's house with its porch light doubled in the puddles, past the shuttered pharmacy. Sienna kept her hands at ten and two as instructed, though her father had told her only last week that real drivers held the wheel loosely, feeling the car answer them rather than commanding it. She had argued with him then, and with Ms. Korhonen in her mind now, two voices insisting on opposite virtues. The wipers beat their patient metronome. "You're doing well," Ms. Korhonen said. "Turn left at the light, and take the long way around the park. The hill floods."

The park road dipped where the storm drains had given up, and the stretch before the underpass lay silver, a wide shallow lake stretching across both lanes. Sienna slowed, eased the wheel, and felt something she had no word for. The steering went weightless under her palms, the car continuing straight while her inputs seemed to reach nothing, as though the wheel had been disconnected and handed to her as a courtesy. Her foot hovered over the brake, which was what every alarmed part of her wanted.

"Don't brake hard," Ms. Korhonen said, quickly but not sharply. "Just ease off the gas. Let the tires find the road again."

Sienna lifted her foot from the accelerator, barely, the way you'd set down a full glass. The engine noise dropped, the car lost speed on its own, and then the wheel came back to her, weight returning to her hands all at once, small ripples of grip as the tires bit down through the water to the asphalt. She steered out of the flooded stretch at an unhurried twenty and did not stop until they had climbed the far side of the dip, where she pulled into the curb beside a row of dripping beech trees and put on the hazards. Her hands were shaking, though her voice was steady.

"What was that? The steering just went away."

"Hydroplaning," Ms. Korhonen said. "Water built up between the tires and the road, so the car lost traction." She said it plainly, the way she named the mirrors and the pedals, and then she let the silence sit, which Sienna appreciated more than any reassurance would have been worth.

They drove home slowly, Sienna turning the moment over. Her father would have said this proved his point, that no checklist could save you when the road turned to water, only feel and nerve; and it was true that the useful thing had happened in her feet, not in a rule. But it was also true that she had known to lift rather than brake because Ms. Korhonen had spoken, and that easing off, letting the tires regain their grip, was itself a kind of instruction, a technique as learnable as ten and two. Perhaps instinct was only procedure that had sunk below the surface of memory. Perhaps the two were not enemies at all. She did not think she could settle it tonight, and strangely that did not bother her; she had the wheel, and the wipers kept their time, and the flooded dip waited behind her to be driven again.

In the driveway her father came out under the eaves with his arms crossed against the rain, and when Sienna told him about the water and the weightless wheel, about lifting her foot and finding the road again, he nodded slowly and said, "So the answer was to do less." Ms. Korhonen laughed from the passenger seat, and Sienna, hands still on the wheel, said, "The answer was to know when."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension means a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher.
story:
The cuff hissed twice before it gave up its answer, and Parker copied the numbers onto the back of a cereal box as though they were homework: 142 over 88. His father sat at the kitchen table with his sleeve still rolled, the machine's plastic arm bandaged around his biceps, and between them lay the pharmacy printout from Tuesday, when a nurse had frowned at the screen and said, "That's stage 2." Parker had been in the waiting area, close enough to hear, far enough to miss the rest, and the phrase had followed him home like a dog he hadn't meant to feed.

His father was convalescing in the loose way the word allowed, doing less than the doctor ordered and more than he wanted, which mostly meant sitting at this table while Parker's mother rearranged the pantry like a woman defusing something. Salt was the first thing exiled. Parker had watched her read labels for an hour, holding a can of soup to the light as if the sodium content might confess under interrogation. That was Thursday. Now it was Saturday morning, and Parker had the cuff, the numbers, and a college pamphlet on nursing open on his lap, though he hadn't decided anything yet.

"Top number's high," his father said, peering at the cereal box. "Bottom one's not so bad."

"I know." Parker didn't actually know, not in the way that counted. He turned the pamphlet over and found the paragraph he'd read four times since Tuesday, the one about the 2017 American guideline, and ran his finger under the words again. Stage 2 hypertension meant a systolic of 140 or higher, or a diastolic of 90 or higher. He said it to himself twice, and something in the grammar of it snagged him, that small repeated word or.

"Either one," he said out loud.

"Either one what?"

"If the top's 140 or more, or the bottom's 90 or more. It doesn't need both. That's why the nurse said stage 2, even though your 88 looked okay." His father chewed on this while rubbing his arm where the cuff had pinched it. Parker wrote 142 ≥ 140 on the box and drew a line to the phrase, feeling the small, unglamorous click of a thing understood. It wasn't the kind of knowledge that impressed anyone at a party. It was the kind that let him stop lying awake constructing disasters out of half-heard sentences.

Derrick had a different theory, delivered over the phone that afternoon while Parker chopped vegetables his mother had left in a symmetrical row. "My uncle cut carbs and his numbers dropped like a rock," Derrick said. "It's all diet, honestly. Exercise is overrated. People just like saying the word lifestyle." Parker diced an onion and thought about how easily Derrick's certainty arrived, how his own mind preferred to hold two explanations at arm's length and let them regard each other. The pamphlet said diet mattered and exercise mattered, and somewhere between the pantry and the sidewalk both of them were true, without either one winning.

He tested the second half that evening. His father walked the loop at the middle school track at a pace that suggested a man negotiating with his own knees, and Parker went with him, partly for company and partly as an experiment he had no intention of calling one. The air smelled of cut grass and the rubber of the old track surface, warm even after sunset. Mathias was there shooting free throws alone under the lights, and he waved without breaking his rhythm, the ball's thud keeping time like a metronome nobody had asked for. After two laps his father's face had color in it, high on the cheeks, and Parker filed that away next to the exiled salt.

Later, over glasses of water because the soda had also been banished, his father said, "Your grandfather never measured anything. Ate what he wanted, worked the orchard, died at eighty-nine." He turned the glass in his hands. "Course, his brother did the same and didn't make fifty. It's a bit capricious, the whole business." Parker nodded, unwilling to say what he suspected, that the numbers were a way of bargaining with exactly that capriciousness, a hedge against fortune dressed up as arithmetic. Ms. Zhou, who taught his stats class, would have called it reducing variance. He'd hated that unit, and now here he was living it.

In bed he read the pamphlet one more time by phone light, then texted Derrick a single question mark in reply to a paragraph about carbs, and left the conversation unresolved the way he was leaving the nursing decision, the way the morning had left 142 over 88: not fine, not catastrophic, holding still in the middle of the range while everything else moved. He set the alarm early, put the cuff on the table beside the cereal box, and turned off the light.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
Alexandre spread the coins across the kitchen table after dinner, heads for the two leads and tails for everyone else. His mother watched from the doorway with a mug in her hand, said nothing, and let him work. The table was the stage. The salt cellar was the doorway where Priya had to enter four lines early, which was the whole problem, because Priya was Khushi's younger sister and Khushi insisted the early entrance ruined the scene.

The one-act belonged to the youth theatre's spring programme, and Ms. Chukwu had handed it to Alexandre with a warning that a director's job was mostly traffic. Two weeks of rehearsal remained. He had never directed anything. On the first night he had stood in the church hall with six actors waiting for him and had said, plausibly, "Maybe just, like, walk around," and Khushi had raised an eyebrow at him from behind the folding table that served as a props desk.

Khushi came over after school on Thursday, dropped her bag on a chair, and leaned over the coins. "Is this what you do instead of eating dinner?"

"It's blocking," Alexandre said. "Where everyone stands and moves." He slid a two-euro coin toward the salt cellar. "But I didn't make that up. Gilbert did it first."

"Which Gilbert?"

"W. S. Gilbert. Nineteenth century. He planned whole scenes on a model stage, and he used a block for each actor. That's where the word comes from." He nudged a one-cent piece an inch left. "I found it in Ms. Chukwu's book on Monday, the one with the cracked spine she keeps on the radiator."

Khushi sat down and studied the arrangement. She was quiet in a way that meant she was deciding whether to argue. "So this is the version where Priya enters at the salt cellar."

"At the line about the letter. Which is later than you want."

"She's standing in the wings for eleven lines doing nothing while two people talk about her."

"They're not talking about her. They're talking about the letter, and the audience doesn't know she's there. That's the point. If she comes in early, she's hovering, and hovering is a kind of begging."

Khushi frowned at the coins as if they had said something rude. Alexandre understood the objection; he had made it to himself all week. A person waiting offstage is dead air. But the scene was an argument between two characters who each believed they were right, and the suddenness of the entrance, mid-sentence, was what made the audience complicit. He had been caught between these two instincts, and it was Koralie, who played the sister with the letter, who had settled it for him on Tuesday without meaning to.

He told Khushi about Tuesday. Koralie had arrived irascible, late from a dentist appointment, and had refused to run the scene the usual way. She wanted to try it faster, angrier, and she had cajoled the other two into dropping all the pauses they had carefully built, and Alexandre, who had been protecting those pauses like a hoarder, had let her. The scene had worked better. The artifice of the long silences, which had felt so literary on the page, turned out to be a wall between the audience and the people on stage. Speed was honest. He still wasn't sure that early entrances worked by the same logic, but he had stopped trusting his instinct that slowness meant depth.

"Priya can enter on the letter line," he said now, "but she enters already moving, like she's been somewhere. Not waiting. I'll mark it on the coins." He picked up the small copper coin and set it beside the salt cellar at a slight angle, facing away, then walked it in a curve toward the two heads.

Khushi turned a coin over with one finger. "And if she hates it?"

"Then we run it both ways Saturday and I watch. Ms. Chukwu says the director watches, that's most of it."

"She also said you'd have to learn to say no."

"I can say no. I'm saying no to hovering."

Khushi laughed, then bent closer and moved the two-euro coin back a step, so that the entrance would cross more of the stage. "More distance," she said. "Let her travel."

Alexandre looked at the new geometry, the copper coin crossing the long diagonal between the two heads, and thought about Gilbert with his model stage, planning people he could lift between two fingers. It was a way of thinking that assumed you could know in advance. He picked up the copper coin and held it, and then he set it down where Khushi had placed it, because she was the one who had to stand in the wings for eleven lines and keep the girl playing her sister alive.

"Saturday," he said. "Tell Priya to bring shoes she can run in."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The first loaf came out of the oven looking like a brick with ambitions, and Brooke set it on the cooling rack knowing before she cut it that she had failed. Her mother was upstairs, still convalescing from the surgery, surviving on toast her father brought up on a tray, and Brooke had wanted tonight to be different. She had wanted to carry up a loaf she had made herself, warm, tearing soft under her mother's fingers. Instead the crumb collapsed into gravelly pieces when she sawed through the crust, and the middle tasted like damp flour. She stood at the counter with the knife in her hand, wondering where it had gone wrong. Too little water, maybe. Or the yeast, which had sat in the cupboard for who knew how long. Or something she hadn't even thought of.

She texted Kendrick, because Kendrick baked the way other people played video games, and he answered her photo of the wreck with a phone call. "You didn't knead it long enough," he said. She could hear a movie playing behind him.

"I kneaded it for ages. Like eight minutes."

"Ages for you is not ages for bread." He was quiet a second, and she imagined him pausing whatever he was watching to think, which for Kendrick was nearly a compliment. "Look up gluten. It's not an ingredient, it's a thing that happens. Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water."

"Proteins," she repeated, writing it on the back of the flour bag because there was nothing else to write on.

"And kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier." He said it the way he said everything, flat and certain, and she believed him, mostly, the way she believed things in textbooks: provisionally, until she could see them work.

The next afternoon her father was at work and the house was quiescent, just the refrigerator hum and the tick of the wall clock, and Brooke measured flour and water and yeast with the fanlight open so the kitchen wouldn't get humid. Halfway through the first rise she let herself drift, remembering her grandmother's kitchen two summers ago, before everything. Her grandmother had kneaded bread without a timer, pushing the dough away with the heel of her hand, folding it back, turning the bowl a quarter rotation, over and over, while she talked about her sister or complained about the price of persimmons. Brooke had been sixteen months younger then and had sat on the counter eating cheese, not watching the hands. She had assumed the bread happened around the talking, not because of it. Now she wondered whether the talking was just what you did to get through the fifteen minutes your hands needed.

She kneaded the second dough until her shoulders burned, counting to a hundred three times, then keeping on past counting because Kendrick had said longer, and longer was the one variable she controlled. The dough changed under her palms, and the change was the kind she wanted to tell somebody about: it stopped being sticky and shaggy and became smooth, elastic, springing back when she poked it, like something that had decided to be alive. She kept working it, curious how far it would go, whether it would tighten forever or reach some limit, and she caught herself smiling at a bowl of flour paste like a person with no dignity, and did not stop.

The loaf rose fat and glossy, and while it baked she did what Kendrick told her not to bother doing and looked it up anyway. The proteins had names she'd already heard from him, glutenin and gliadin, and she read a paragraph about networks with the oven clock ticking in her ear, and she understood roughly half of it, which felt like enough to work with. What she kept turning over was the idea that nothing in the bowl was gluten until water arrived. Two things sitting inert in the flour, and then a third thing, ordinary tap water, and then a structure that hadn't existed a moment before. She thought of her mother's friend Denise, who kept saying that after the surgery nothing would go back to how it was, as if that were the final word on the subject. Brooke didn't have an argument against it exactly. She only had the sense, standing in the flour dust, that combining things was not the same as losing them.

Ashleigh came over while the bread cooled, drawn by the smell, and cut a slice against Brooke's protests that it was supposed to rest. "It's chewy," Ashleigh said, through the chew. "Like, really chewy."

"That's the point. Probably." Brooke tore her own piece and pulled it, watching the crumb stretch into threads instead of crumbling. Dense first, chewy second, and the difference had been fifteen more minutes of her own hands, which meant the failure had been hers and so was the fix. Whether more kneading would have made it better still, or past some point worse, she honestly didn't know, and she said so. Ashleigh said that was a weird thing to be pleased about.

She carried the loaf upstairs on the good cutting board, still warm through the wood, and knocked with her elbow. Her mother was propped against the pillows with the blinds half drawn, and she said, "You made that?" in a voice Brooke decided not to analyze. Brooke cut a thick slice, buttered it, and held it out.

"Careful," she said. "It's chewier than it looks."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: An overvote happens when a voter marks more choices than a contest allows, and that vote is not counted for that contest.
story:
The desks had been shoved against the wall, and in their place stood three folding tables with cardboard voting booths behind them, which Mr. Ionescu had borrowed from the county and installed in the classroom with the solemnity of a man setting up an altar. Mackenzie stood at the check-in table beside Maya, a stack of stubby pencils at her elbow and the voter roster in front of her. The election was real, at least within the walls of the school: student council president, a referendum on the late-start proposal, ballots printed by the district office and counted by a scanner that Mr. Ionescu had promised to bring back from the fire hall after the real election in November. He had told them, more than once, that democracy was a muscle, and that muscles left unused would atrophy. He had said it so often that Tiffany had started whispering the word at odd moments, flexing her arm in the aisle.

The lines formed after fourth period. Mackenzie found the names, checked them off, handed each voter a ballot in its gray sleeve, and pointed them toward a booth. It was repetitive work, and she was surprised by how much she liked it, the small ceremony of it, the way even the kids who usually knocked chairs over walked softly once they were holding a ballot, as though the paper itself demanded something.

Tiffany came through the line on her way to lunch and lingered at the table, leaning close. "You know Dara's telling everyone to vote for both candidates," she said. "Like, both. She says it's, like, a protest, that neither one deserves a whole vote." Tiffany rolled her eyes, but she was grinning, the way she grinned when a rumor was good.

"That's not a protest," Maya said without looking up from the roster. "That's just wasting a vote."

"It's a statement."

"It's a spoiled ballot."

Mackenzie said nothing, because a freshman was standing in front of her holding his ballot sleeve the wrong way, and she had to show him where the seal went.

The trouble came twenty minutes later, near the end of lunch. A boy named Elias, a senior Mackenzie knew only as someone who argued with referees at basketball games, came out of the booth holding his ballot at arm's length, like something that might bite. He fed it into the scanner, and the machine spat it back with a low mechanical complaint and a message on its small screen that Mackenzie couldn't read from the table. Mr. Ionescu was across the room helping a girl whose booth had collapsed. Elias fed the ballot in again. The machine refused it again, and now his neck had gone red.

"What's wrong with this thing," he said, not quite a question.

Mackenzie left the check-in table, because it was hers to leave; she was the clerk for that station. At the scanner she could see the ballot through the plastic feed tray. For president, the oval beside one candidate was filled in, and so was the oval beside the other. Two dark marks, side by side, in a contest that allowed one choice.

"You marked two for president," she said.

"So? That means I hate both of them less than I hate, whatever." He shrugged. "Count it for both."

"It doesn't work that way." She had read the poll worker guide the night before, the thin booklet Mr. Ionescu had photocopied, and she found the line now the way you find a handhold in the dark. "It's called an overvote. You marked more choices than the contest allows, so your vote doesn't get counted for that contest."

"The whole ballot's dead?"

She checked. "No. President's not counted. Everything else still counts." She looked at the rest of his ballot, at the late-start referendum where he had filled one oval, and at the class officer races below it. "You can take a new ballot and start over, if you want. You're allowed."

Elias stood there for a moment, jaw working. Down the table, Tiffany was watching, and Maya was watching, and behind them a short line was forming. "Then what was the point of filling it in," he said, and it wasn't really directed at anyone.

Mackenzie thought of Maya's certainty, the vote as a thing you either used correctly or wasted, and of what Elias had been trying to do, which was to register something true, that he didn't want either of them, and there was no box for that. She didn't think either of them was entirely wrong, and she didn't know how to say so in the time she had. There was a line behind him and a machine beeping and a book of rules in her head that told her exactly what she was permitted to do, which was offer him one fresh ballot, and nothing about what she should tell him to do with it.

"Sometimes the point is just that you showed up," she said, and heard how thin it sounded.

Elias took the fresh ballot. He went back into the booth and was in there a long time, long enough that the line murmured, and when he came out he fed the new ballot into the scanner and it slid through clean. Mackenzie couldn't see his marks and didn't try to. He walked past the check-in table without looking at anyone, and Tiffany leaned over to Maya and whispered, loud enough to be heard, "So did he pick one, or did he do it again?"

"Read the tape," Maya said, and pointed at the scanner's paper tally, which was still printing, curling out of the machine like a slow answer neither of them had asked for.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually do not include sales tax, which is added at the register, so the total is higher than the posted price.
story:
Gabrielle counted the bills again in the parking lot, six of them, ten dollars each, folded into her jacket pocket like a secret. The sneakers in the window of Alder's Sports had been there since September, priced at fifty-four ninety-nine, and today she had finally saved enough. She pushed through the door past a rack of clearance jerseys and found the shoes on the bottom shelf, grey and blue, her size according to the sticker, and carried them to the register where a bored cashier was restocking gum.

"Fifty-four ninety-nine," the cashier said, scanning the box, "plus tax, so it comes to sixty-one point one two."

Gabrielle stood very still. She laid out five tens, then the sixth, and waited for the register to tell her what she already suspected. The screen showed a total higher than the sticker, a difference of more than six dollars, and her money was short. "There's tax on top?" she asked. "On the price that's already on the box?"

"That's how it works here," the cashier said, not unkindly. "The shelf price doesn't include it. It gets added at the register." He held the box to one side, patient in the way of someone who had watched this exact scene many times.

She asked him to wait, and stepped toward the benches by the changing rooms where Mickael was sitting, scrolling his phone. He worked Saturdays at the garden centre and had been telling her for weeks about his paycheques, how the number he earned and the number that reached his bank account never matched. She had half listened, the way you half listen to someone describing a country you've never visited. Now she crouched beside him. "Can I borrow seven dollars? I'll pay you Friday."

"For the shoes?" He looked at the box, then at her face. "Yeah. Okay. But you know you'll owe me more than seven by the time you're done." He was joking, mostly, but he followed her back to the register and counted out the coins.

While the cashier rang it through, Gabrielle watched the receipt spool out of the printer, longer than she expected, itemized. The subtotal, then a line for sales tax, then the total, each number in its own row like a small argument being settled in public. "They print it right there," she said. "Like a confession."

Mickael laughed. "Wait till you see my pay stub. It's a whole page of confessions." He pulled up a photo on his phone, a dense grid of abbreviations, and tilted the screen so she could see. There was his gross pay, and beneath it a stack of deductions with names like federal income tax and provincial income tax and something called EI, each one taking its slice, until the net pay at the bottom sat there like the last cookie on a plate. "I thought my first cheque would be four hundred and eighty," he said. "It was four hundred and six. That first week I did the math on the bus like four times."

Gabrielle took her receipt and folded it into the same pocket where the bills had been, the two papers resting against each other, one showing what she'd paid and one showing what he'd earned, both of them smaller than the number printed at the top. "So everywhere you turn," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke, "there's the number you see first, and then there's the real number. The sticker is one thing and the register is another. Your wage is one thing and your paycheque is another."

"That's one way to put it." Mickael pocketed his phone. "My dad calls it the difference between gross and net. He says you should always do the math before you agree to anything." He said it lightly, but Gabrielle noticed he said it like a person who had done the math wrong once and remembered.

They walked out past the window where her sneakers had lived since September, the empty space on the shelf already occupied by a different box, someone else's wanting. In the food court next door, Greta was saving a table, waving them over, and Gabrielle went to the counter with the last crumpled two dollars from her pocket, intending a drink. The board said the lemonade was one ninety-nine. She had learned something in the last half hour, though, and before handing over her money she asked the cashier, "What's the total after tax?"

"Two twenty-three."

She counted her coins on the counter, came up short by a quarter, and stood there deciding whether to be embarrassed or delighted that she had known enough to ask. Greta appeared beside her with a quarter already extended in her palm, having watched the whole transaction from the table. "You looked like you were bracing for something," Greta said.

"I was bracing for the register." Gabrielle took the coin and paid, and when the receipt printed she held it up beside the shoe receipt in her other hand, comparing the two columns of small numbers, the tax listed on both, honest and unapologetic. She thought of Mr. Ma, who ran the corner store near school and had once let her take a milk carton when she was a dollar short, telling her the tax would still be there tomorrow so she might as well learn its face today. At the time it had sounded like a riddle. Now it sounded like the plainest sentence in the world.

The three of them sat with their drinks, and Gabrielle slid the shoe box out of its bag and put the sneakers on right there at the table, lacing them while Greta narrated the fashion show and Mickael filmed ten seconds of it for his story. The shoes fit. She flexed her feet against the food court floor and felt the new stiffness that would soften into hers within a week.

"So was it worth the extra?" Greta asked, nodding at the receipts still fanned out on the table.

"I don't know yet." Gabrielle gathered the papers together and squared their edges. "It cost more than the sticker said, and I still don't get why the sticker can't just say the real number. But at least now when I see a price, I hear the register underneath it." She tucked the receipts into the box, under the tissue paper, alongside the shoes. "Mickael, on Friday, do you want me to pay you back the seven, or the seven plus what the tax on seven would be?"

He grinned over his drink. "Pay me back the seven and I'll absorb the rest."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Raising interest rates tends to strengthen a country's currency by attracting foreign savings, which makes imports cheaper and puts downward pressure on prices.
story:
The mower had died in the middle of the back lawn, and her grandfather had gone inside for water, so Savannah sat on the porch steps of their house with her laptop balanced on her knees and the spreadsheet open. Six months of babysitting money, plus the graduation cheques, plus whatever she could earn at the garden centre until August. The numbers were closer than she had expected. The hotel in Seoul, converted from won to dollars, had actually gotten cheaper since she'd first priced the trip in the spring, and she had no idea why.

"You're frowning at a screen," her grandmother said, setting down two glasses of lemonade. "Is it money or a boy?"

"It's money. The exchange rate got better for us. I thought trips only got more expensive." Behind them, the sprinkler ticked across the flowerbeds, and somewhere down the block Ms. Park's dog was barking at the mail carrier again.

Her grandmother lowered herself into the wicker chair and said, "A strong dollar. Your grandfather complains about it every time he looks at his retirement account, and then he remembers it helps when we travel, and then he complains again."

That evening Vera called about the itinerary, and Alix got patched in, and the three of them argued about palaces versus night markets until Alix, in that sardonic voice she saved for Savannah specifically, said, "You realize you can't actually explain any of this. You're going to stand up in Ms. Park's class on Thursday and tell us why the central bank raised rates, and you don't even know why your own hotel got cheaper."

"I know the first part," Savannah said. "Rates go up, loans cost more, people and businesses borrow less, they spend less, and prices stop climbing so fast. That's the whole thing."

"Then why did the currency move?"

She didn't have an answer, and she hated not having an answer, and Alix knew it, and the call ended with Vera promising to bring printed maps and Alix promising nothing. Savannah lay in the guest room under the sloped ceiling, listening to the house settle, and decided that if the connection existed, she would find it before Thursday. It was not really about Thursday. It was that Alix had found the seam in her understanding and pulled at it, and now the whole garment felt loose.

The next morning her grandfather drove her to the library in town, where she sat between a man reading the funeral notices and two kids sharing one headphone, and she read everything she could find, and most of it assumed she already understood the part she didn't. When she got back, her grandmother was at the kitchen table sorting a shoebox of old papers, and there was a folded newspaper clipping from years ago, kept because her grandfather's name appeared in it, about a local credit union. Savannah read the headline twice. Then she asked her grandmother what she remembered about that year.

"Everyone was upset about their mortgages," her grandmother said, cutting a length of twine. "But I remember being pleased with myself, because our savings finally paid something. And I remember the man at the bank saying money had come in from overseas. Foreign savers wanted our rates too." She tied the twine around a bundle of letters. "Money went where it was treated well. It always does."

Savannah sat very still. Foreign savers, bringing their money in, meant more demand for the currency. A stronger currency. She pulled up the spreadsheet on her phone and looked again at the hotel price, the identical number of won now costing fewer dollars than it had in March. A stronger dollar made imports cheaper. Cheaper imports pressed down on prices, the same direction as the expensive-loan story she had already learned, another channel running alongside the first. It wasn't a different theory. It was the same outcome arriving by a second road. She said it out loud, slowly, testing each link in the chain while her grandmother watched her over the shoebox, and each link held.

"Congratulations," her grandmother said. "You look like your grandfather when the mower finally starts."

On Thursday, Savannah stood at the front of Ms. Park's classroom with her notes face down on the desk, because she had decided she could say it without them. She explained the borrowing channel first, the way she had understood it all along. Then she said, "But that's not the only path. When rates rise, foreign savers bring their money in to earn those rates, and that strengthens our currency. A stronger currency makes imports cheaper, and cheaper imports put downward pressure on prices." She looked at Alix, who was leaning back with her arms crossed, and waited. Alix uncrossed her arms first.

"That actually works," Alix admitted. "Fine. That works."

After class, Vera caught up with them in the corridor with the printed maps flapping like a sail. "So we can afford the better hotel now? Is that what all this was about?"

"One thing I still can't tell you," Savannah said, folding the maps neatly in half. "Whether they'll raise rates again before we fly."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homophily, a term from sociologists Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton in 1954, is the tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves.
story:
The moving truck left tire marks in the fresh asphalt of Kessler Court, and Samantha stood on the porch of a house that was not yet hers, holding a box labeled in her mother's handwriting, a handwriting she had not seen on anything belonging to her before. The street was new in every sense: the lawns were seeded mud, the saplings were staked like patients learning to stand, and the houses had that unweathered sameness of places built all at once.
