Ms. Fernando from next door crossed the gap between driveways with a plate of lemon squares and an appraising look. "You'll want to know which houses have kids your age," she said. "Third one down has a girl, senior year I think. And the corner house, the loud one, two boys." Samantha thanked her and carried the box inside, where the echo made everything sound borrowed.

Morgan had promised to text every night, and for the first three nights she did. The messages arrived with the old shorthand intact, the abbreviations Samantha could read like her own pulse, and then the fourth night produced nothing, and the fifth produced a photograph of a party Samantha had not been invited to, sent apparently by accident, or perhaps not. She lay on her unmade bed in a room that still smelled of paint and read the photograph the way an archaeologist might exhume a fragment: three faces, one table, a constellation of people she knew clustered around people like them.

School started on a Tuesday. The cafeteria was a plain of long tables, and Samantha understood within ninety seconds of standing in the lunch line that the room had already organized itself without her input. Band kids at the far window, their instrument cases stacked like luggage. Runners in technical fabric, eating as though fueling. Gamers around a single screen someone had propped against a milk carton. It was not hostile, this arrangement; it was simply complete, a finished puzzle into which she had not been cut.

"You're staring," said a girl beside her in line, dark bangs, a library copy of a physics text under her arm. "Everybody stares their first day. I did." Her name was Frederique, and she had moved here in tenth grade, which she described as "the year I learned that being new is a skill you forget immediately." She ate alone, she admitted, not out of principle but out of arithmetic. "Homophily," she said, tapping the cover of her book. "Sociologists, Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton, 1954. It's the tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves. I found it when I was trying to figure out why nobody here talked to me." She said it lightly, the way you report the weather, and then asked Samantha what she was into.

The honest answer was everything and nothing defensible: books, yes, but also track, which she had quit junior year, and the debate team, which had felt like home until it hadn't. She gave Frederique the partial version, and Frederique nodded and said the partial version was what everyone gave, that the full version was reserved for people you'd known for years, which was precisely the problem, since the only way to know people for years was to start somewhere. They sat at a table for two by the vending machines. A boy from the gamers' table looked over once, then returned to the screen. Samantha noticed that she kept checking the door, some reflexive hope that a familiar face would walk through it, though the nearest familiar face was a hundred and ten miles away.

That night Morgan called, finally, and the conversation had the gait of two people walking the same route at different speeds. "You should come visit," Samantha said, and Morgan said maybe at Thanksgiving, and the maybe sat between them on the line like a third party neither wanted to acknowledge. After they hung up, Samantha felt petulant about it, small and sulky in a way she disliked in herself, and she tried to locate the fairness in the situation and could not. Morgan had not moved. Morgan's world had not been uprooted and replanted in a development with saplings for neighbors. It was not Morgan's job to grieve a change that had been done to Samantha and not to her, and yet Samantha wanted her to grieve it anyway, and knew the wanting was unjust, and wanted it anyway.

Frederique turned out to be an autodidact of the most thorough kind, self-taught in calculus and card tricks and the history of narrow-gauge railroads, and their lunches acquired a rhythm. Samantha learned that Frederique had tried the runners' table once, in tenth grade, and had been absorbed into the conversation for exactly one afternoon before the talk turned to times and splits and she had nothing to contribute, and similarity, it seemed, was not only about interest but about vocabulary, about the particular dialect each group spoke. This made Samantha think of the photograph from the party, how the faces had not been doing anything she could not have done, only doing it together, in their shared language, from which she had been edited out by distance rather than by choice.

By the third week she had done something she had not planned: she joined the new debate club, which met in a portable classroom and drew exactly five students, two of whom, she suspected, were there for the free snacks. Ms. Fernando, who taught across town and recognized her at a school event, said, "So you found your people," and Samantha started to agree and then stopped, because it wasn't quite that. She had found a people, small and provisional and assembled by chance rather than chemistry, and the distinction mattered to her in a way she could not yet articulate. Homophily was real; she had watched it arrange a cafeteria in real time. But it was also a description, not a law, and the difference between the two was the difference between a map and a fence.

On a Saturday in October, Morgan texted a photograph of nothing in particular, the two of them absent from it, and Samantha understood that the old tie was thinning in the manner of all ties not fed, and that some of this was distance and some of it was simply that they had been similar in the environment that made them, and the environment had changed. She sat on the porch of the house that was now hers, in the neighborhood that was slowly becoming hers, eating a lemon square from a new batch Ms. Fernando had left on the railing. Down the street, the girl from the third house was chalking something on her driveway, huge looping letters too far away to read, and Samantha pulled on her shoes and walked toward them to see what they said.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: A 2001 review titled 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good', led by Roy Baumeister, found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size.
story:
Dinner on Sunday began, as it always did, with her father asking each of them for the worst moment of the week, which he called keeping the books balanced. Gabriella pushed rice around her plate and said the worst moment was telling Shyla she was dropping the baton too early in the relay exchange.

"That doesn't sound so terrible," her mother said.

"It was the other part. The part where she stopped talking to me."

Her mother ladled more stew into her brother's bowl and changed the subject to the boiler, which had begun making a sound her father described as querulous, a thin complaining whine that came and went with the pilot light. Gabriella let the conversation pass over her. In her head she was replaying Tuesday on the track: she had said Shyla's stride looked stronger, her starts were faster, her arm carriage had improved, her pacing in the second lap was smarter than anyone's, and then, at the end, that she was releasing the baton a half-second early and costing them the exchange. Five good things and one bad thing. She had counted them on the walk home, pleased with her generosity. Shyla had walked to the far side of the parking lot with her hood up and had not sat with her at lunch since.

After dinner she found Rami at the library table by the windows, where he did his chemistry homework every Sunday. She told him the whole thing, the five compliments and the one criticism, and how the five had vanished like breath off glass.

"It's not just Shyla," Rami said. He turned his binder around to show a page of notes he'd copied from a psychology book for an essay. "There's a review from 2001 led by Roy Baumeister, and it's literally called 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good.' They found that negative events and remarks usually hit people harder than positive ones of about the same size."

"Same size," Gabriella repeated.

"One to one. A bad thing and a good thing, equally big. The bad one leaves the deeper mark."

She sat with that. It should have made her feel better about Shyla's silence, and it did, briefly, the way any explanation feels like absolution. But by the time she'd walked home under the wet trees, she had begun to wonder whether she was using it to litigate her own innocence rather than to fix anything. She could build a case that she'd done nothing wrong, five exhibits of kindness against one count of honesty, and win it, and still have no partner for the relay on Thursday. The postulate she'd been working from, that feedback was a ledger you balanced by volume, might simply be wrong. Maybe one criticism did weigh as much as five compliments, and maybe the answer wasn't to hold back the criticism, but to make it so small and so precise that it couldn't be mistaken for a verdict on the whole person.

On Monday she caught Shyla at the fence after practice, before she could get her hood up.

"I said it wrong last week," Gabriella said. "I piled everything good into a heap and buried the one thing you actually needed. It sounded like a setup, like all of it was there to soften the blow."

Shyla studied a point somewhere past the goalposts.

"So here it is plain. Your second exchange, the one where you hand off to Adele. You open your hand at the second cone instead of the third. That's it. Everything else is genuinely good and I meant all of it."

Shyla turned her water bottle in her hands. "I thought you were going to tell me I shouldn't be on the relay at all."

"What? No."

"You listed all that stuff first, like a lawyer. I kept waiting for the part where you said I was the problem." She unzipped her bag and took out her spikes. "Second cone instead of third. I can see that. Coach always yells 'wait, wait' at me and I never knew what she meant."

They walked to the bus loop together, and Gabriella, feeling lighter than she had all week, made the mistake of saying so. "See, it's not so bad being told something specific."

"No," Shyla said. "It's not." Then, as the bus hissed up to the curb, she added, "Yours is your takeoff foot. You false start against people with quick triggers, like Adele. Everyone knows. Nobody wanted to say it because you're the one who gives the talks about taking feedback."

Gabriella stood there while the doors folded shut and Shyla waved from a window seat, and she caught herself, mid-sting, doing exactly what she had spent the week reading about: forgetting every smooth warm thing, holding only the small sharp true one.

"Second cone," she called through the glass anyway. "Third, I mean. I'll wait for the third."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
I am, by my own admission, the most organized person in this library, which is why I had spread my supplies across an entire table by four o'clock: three sketchbooks, a shoebox of pencils sorted by grade, a bone folder I'd expropriated from my mother's wrapping-paper drawer without her noticing, and the half-finished zine that was due at the art showcase on Friday. I say half-finished. It was more like an eighth-finished, but I've always believed in rounding up.

The project was a hand-bound booklet of graphite portraits, twelve pages, printed nowhere, photocopied nowhere, entirely original, which was the whole point. Mr. Malik, the librarian who had approved my booking of the big table by the window, had one rule: no paint, no ink, nothing that could permanently improve the furniture. Graphite suited me fine. Graphite was my whole personality, according to Tamara, who arrived at four-thirty and dropped her sketchbook onto my carefully sorted pencil tray like a meteor.

"Fix this," she said. Her drawing of Kolton was actually good, which annoyed me, but the whole page had gone gray and ghostly, the shadows smeared sideways as if the portrait had been caught in a small landslide.

"You're dragging your hand through it," I said, which is what a confident expert says. I was not yet an expert, a fact I will admit now that no showcase judge is reading over my shoulder.

"You're the pencil guy," she said. "Which pencil did I use? You have forty of them."

I looked at the pencil she'd left clipped to the page. It said 6B on the barrel. I picked up one of mine, an HB, then a 2H, and made three short strokes on scrap paper side by side. The 2H came out pale and crisp. The HB came out medium. The 6B, when I tested it, came out black and soft and promptly smudged when I ran a thumb over it. Huh, I thought, in those exact eloquent words.

"So?" Tamara said.

"So a pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay," I said, mostly to myself, arranging the three test strokes like evidence. "More clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H. Less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B. You used a 6B. You basically drew Kolton with charcoal wearing a trench coat."

"You're making that up."

"Am I the sort of person who makes things up?"

"Yes," said Kolton himself, arriving behind her with a slushie, which was against library policy, though Mr. Malik only gave it a long, disappointed look from the desk, like a parent at a graduation where the speaker has gone overtime. "Constantly. Last week he told me the bone folder was for folding bones."

I handed Tamara the 2H anyway. "Try your darks with this, then layer. It'll hold still."

She redrew the shadow under Kolton's jaw, and it stayed put, sharp as a folded edge. I felt the specific, embarrassing pleasure of having been accidentally right. We worked for an hour, and I got two more portrait pages done, or one and a half, fine, one and a quarter, and then Mr. Malik came by with a note, because Mr. Malik believes talking above a murmur erodes the foundations of the building.

The note read: "Reserved tables revert to the library at 6 p.m. However, the study room by the periodicals is free until closing, and it has a larger table. This is not altruistic of me; you left pencil shavings on the carpet last Tuesday and I want you where I can watch you. P.S. Tell the young woman her drawing is better than yours. Signed, a misanthrope with a broom."

"He's not wrong," Kolton said, reading over my shoulder. "About the drawing, I mean. The misanthrope part too, possibly."

We moved everything to the study room, which did have a larger table, and Tamara spread her pages out beside mine so we could compare shadow techniques like rival scientists, except friendly, and except that her Kolton portrait was, annoyingly, better than my Kolton portrait even after the smudge repair. At some point she picked up my 4B without asking, and I let her, because a person can only guard so many pencils before he becomes the sort of person who guards pencils.

"Twelve pages by Friday," she said. "You have one and a quarter."

"One and a half. There's one in my bag."

"There's a grocery list in your bag."

"It's a conceptual grocery list." I sharpened the 2H with my mother's stolen bone folder, which does not sharpen pencils, as it turns out, and Tamara laughed so hard Mr. Malik opened the study room door, broom in hand, and pointed at the clock.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
Grace had told her mother, twice, that she knew exactly what she was going to say, which was the first sign that she did not. The kinara sat on the folding table beside the sweet potato pie, three red candles, one black in the center, three green, and Grace's grandmother had announced, in the tone she reserved for sentencing, that Grace would explain the day's principle before the candle was lit. That was an hour ago. Since then Grace had composed four speeches in her head and abandoned all of them on the walk from the parking lot, past the coatrack and the folding chairs, into the basement of the church where her family had held the gathering every December for as long as she could remember, which, as she would admit only later, was part of the problem.

The basement smelled of fried plantains and floor wax and the particular cold of concrete that never fully warms. Her cousin Jalen, age six, was conducting an orchestra of plastic dinosaurs under the punch bowl. Her uncle was arguing with the deacon about whether the Flyers needed a new coach, an argument that had been running, in one form or another, since roughly the Pleistocene, and showed every sign of being atavistic in the way certain family disputes are: not learned so much as inherited, flaring up each December like a rash.

"Grace." Her grandmother did not raise her voice. She had never needed to. "We're ready for you, baby."

Grace stood up. She was, by her own account, an excellent public speaker; she had given the graduation address in June and her father still played the video for guests, which several people could confirm and none of them would, because the video had in fact cut out forty seconds in when the battery died, and Grace had never corrected him. She smoothed her dress and walked to the front of the room and looked at thirty faces, most of them chewing.

"Today's the first day," she said. "December twenty-sixth. The first candle is black, and it's for Umoja, which means unity." So far, so good; this part she had looked up that morning on her phone while brushing her teeth, hunched over the sink like a raccoon. "Kwanzaa goes from December twenty-sixth through January first, and there are seven principles, one for each day. Umoja comes first." She paused, because here was where the speeches had diverged. Speech three had been about her grandmother's hands. Speech two had been about forgiveness, and she had scrapped it after remembering that she and Ember were currently not speaking.

Ember was in the third row. Grace had not expected that; Ember's mother was Grace's mother's cousin, so technically family, but Ember hadn't come in three years, not since the incident at the Christmas pageant, which Grace still maintained she could not be blamed for, and which everyone else in the room had apparently decided to treat as a historical event requiring a formal detente rather than a conversation. Ember was wearing her green coat and eating plantains with the focus of a person pretending not to be watched.

"Unity means," Grace said, and her mind offered, unhelpfully, nothing.

"You could mention when it started," her mother offered gently, from the side.

"Right. It was created in nineteen sixty-six by Maulana Karenga." She had read this perhaps ninety seconds before her grandmother called her name, and she said it now with the borrowed authority of someone quoting a phone. "So it's not ancient. It's newer than Mom." A ripple of laughter, some of it from her mother, who mouthed something that was probably not biblical. "And I used to think that made it, like, less real. My friend Lucy has traditions that are a thousand years old, and I'm standing here explaining something younger than the Flyers' championship drought." Uncle Ray pointed at her with his cup, either in agreement or threat. "But I don't think that anymore. Mostly."

She looked at the kinara, the unlit black candle waiting in its center.

"Here's what I actually think. Unity isn't something you have because you're related to people in a church basement eating pie. It's something you do, badly, over and over. This year I didn't do it very well. I stopped talking to somebody in this room for eleven months over something stupid, and instead of calling her I just waited for her to call me, and we both got very good at waiting." Ember put down her plantain. Grace's heart was doing something arrhythmic and embarrassing. "I can't predicate a whole holiday on one apology, and I'm not going to stand up here and say everything's fine, because you'd all know I was lying and my grandmother can smell a lie through a casserole."

"True," said her grandmother.

"But the candle's for Umoja. Unity. Day one of seven, and January first is a long way off, and I figure if I'm honest today, maybe by the last day I'll have earned one of the other principles, whichever one is about being a decent person." She turned to the kinara. "I don't actually know which one that is yet. I'm going to look it up."

The room laughed, and her grandmother lit the black candle, and the flame caught and leaned sideways under the ceiling fan, and Grace, walking back to her seat, stopped at the third row.

Ember pulled out the empty chair beside her without looking up. "The one about purpose," she said. "You're thinking of the one about purpose."

"Is that day two?"

"Day four. I Googled it in October, waiting for you to call." She pushed the plate of plantains across, still not looking, and Grace sat down and took one, and the candle burned on behind them, small and stubborn, at the front of the room where everyone could see it.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
Jaxon's grandfather lived four streets from the gurdwara, close enough that on festival mornings the sound of the kirtan drifted into the kitchen where his mother was already pressing the good kurta into his hands. The shirt smelled of iron and cardamom from the cupboard. He held it without putting it on.

"You're bringing the girl from your class," his mother said. Not a question.

"Roxane. She wanted to come. She's doing a project on, like, community traditions." That was half true. Roxane had said she was curious, and curious for Roxane meant she wanted to film everything, and Jaxon had not decided yet whether that was a problem.

Roxane arrived at the grandfather's house in a borrowed scarf, holding it wrong, wound twice around her throat like she was cold. The grandfather, Nanaji, looked at it, looked at her sneakers, and said nothing, which Jaxon understood as a verdict. He took a spare rumal from the hall drawer, a plain blue one, and folded it for her the way he'd been taught at eight, corners meeting corners.

"Is there a fee for entry?" Roxane asked on the walk over. "Or a donation thing?"

"No. After, there's food. That's the part I want you to see." He stopped at the gate, where shoes came off in heaps. "The langar. It's free, it's vegetarian, and it doesn't matter who you are. Religion, caste, none of it. Everyone sits on the floor together."

"Together how?"

"You'll see." Landyn had texted him twice already that morning, the second message calling the whole thing antiquated, sitting on the ground like peasants, and Jaxon had typed three replies and deleted all of them. Landyn talked that way about everything he hadn't done, as if refusing to enter a room made him an authority on what was inside it. Jaxon knew the opposite posture was its own trap, the solipsism of assuming his own family's rituals were self-evidently meaningful to a stranger. Roxane was not his grandmother. He could not hand her his reverence like a coat.

Inside, the hall was loud with harmonium and bodies. Roxane held her phone low, filming the canopy, the gold of the palki, and an older woman in a blue salwar kameez touched Roxane's elbow and pointed at the screen, then at her own eyes, gentle but unmistakable. Roxane put the phone away. Jaxon watched her palms flatten in front of her chest as the sangat passed, her mouth moving along with sounds she didn't know, and he felt something he hadn't expected, which was that her clumsiness made the room more real to him, not less. He had been coming here since before he could rank the parts. She was ranking them now, and her attention instantiated something he'd been performing without examining: the meal was coming, and he wanted to watch her receive it.

The langar hall smelled of dal and hot steel. They lined up with trays and took bread from a woman whose forearm shone with steam. "Take more," she told Roxane, who had taken almost none. "You look hungry." Roxane laughed, caught out, and took more.

They sat on the floor in rows, cross-legged, shoulder to shoulder with strangers, and Roxane leaned in to whisper, "There's a guy in a full suit down there. And that family over there looks like they came from a wedding."

"Yeah."

"So it's everyone."

"That's the whole point. Equal, on the floor." He said it and heard his own voice, and it didn't sound like an explanation. It sounded like something he'd just confirmed. For years he'd absorbed his mother's version, that the langar was about humility and service, and Landyn's version, that the floor was a humiliation dressed up as virtue, and he had never made himself sit between the two long enough to decide. Now Roxane was eating with both hands, and the man in the suit was passing her the water jug without being asked, and neither of them seemed to be performing anything. Jaxon still didn't know what he believed about the prayers upstairs, the part with his eyes closed. He knew this part, though, or he knew it better than he had at breakfast.

His grandfather appeared at the end of their row with a cloth in his hands, wiping spilled dal off the floor beside a child, and then, without breaking motion, sitting down beside Roxane with his own tray. He didn't greet them. He tore his bread and looked at her plate.

"Eat," Nanaji said. "There is always more."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs, while an endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter.
story:
The library at four o'clock had a spartan feel to it, most of the chairs stacked, the tall windows throwing long rectangles of light across the empty tables. John spread his sources across the largest one: three photocopied pages, a library book with a cracked spine, his laptop open to a document that was mostly a title and one brave sentence about the Transcontinental Railroad.

He had argued with his father about it at breakfast. His father wanted the paper on the railroad as progress, the thing everyone lionized in fourth-grade units, the iron spine of a nation. John had found a photocopy of an 1868 editorial complaining that Chinese laborers were paid less than white workers for the same blasting work, and he wanted to write about that instead. His father had said, "Pick a thesis you can prove." John still wasn't sure that was the same as picking a thesis that was true.

Lina dropped into the chair across from him with her own laptop and a look of controlled panic. "The paper's due Thursday."

"Mine too."

"Look at this." She turned her screen toward him. At the bottom of her last printed page, a thin rule and nothing beneath it. On a final page, a column of small numbers had gathered like birds on a wire. "They were at the bottoms of the pages yesterday. Now they're all at the end. Did I break it?"

John leaned in. He'd spent half of Sunday with the style guide open, mostly because he'd gotten a footnote wrong on the first draft and Mr. Littlechild had circled it in red and written "check your format" in handwriting like fence wire. Since then he'd read the section on notes twice, partly to avoid reading the section on plagiarism.

"Those are endnotes now," he said.

"Is that a problem?"

"They're not the same thing. A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs. An endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper."

Lina stared at the page as if it had moved furniture behind her back. "So which one am I supposed to have?"

"Depends on the style. What did Mr. Littlechild ask for?"

She scrolled through the assignment sheet. "Chicago. Footnotes or endnotes." She read it twice. "It says or."

"So it's allowed."

"Then why did the program move them?"

"Setting," John said, and took her laptop before she could answer. He found it under References, a dropdown that offered footnotes or endnotes, and a checkbox that had switched itself when she'd changed margins. He switched it back. "Try printing one page."

She did. The note sat at the bottom of the page, small and correct, attached to its sentence like a shadow. She exhaled.

Adelyn arrived with a hockey bag over one shoulder and dropped it against the shelf. "You two are still here."

"Footnotes," Lina said, as if that explained a war.

Adelyn pulled up a chair anyway and looked at John's spread of pages. "What's yours on?"

"The railroad. Sort of both sides."

"Both sides of what?"

"The textbook says the railroad united the country. This editorial says the men who built the western section were paid by ethnicity, not by work." He slid the photocopy toward her. "I want to use the textbook as a counterpoint. Show what everyone believed at the time, then show this."

Adelyn read the photocopy quickly, the way she read everything, like a scout. "So your thesis is the editorial?"

"I don't know yet." He heard how weak it sounded and kept going anyway. "One editorial isn't a pattern. One newspaper guy being angry isn't evidence the whole thing was rotten. If I write it like the editorial proves something, that's worse than writing nothing."

"Then write what you can prove," Adelyn said, "and say what you can't."

Lina laughed once, surprised. "That's allowed?"

"It's called an argument," Adelyn said. "Not a verdict."

John looked at his document, at its single brave sentence, and began deleting it. He typed a new first line, slower, pausing between clauses. Then he set a footnote marker after the editorial's title and filled in the citation, checking the model in the style guide twice, then a third time, until the commas fell in the right places.

Lina packed up first, her pages stacked and square. At the door she turned. "Thanks. Seriously."

He waved without looking up. The library lights went to half, the closing signal, and he kept typing, the note riding at the bottom of the page where he had put it.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Plain-language guidance recommends the active voice, in which the subject does the action, as in 'I missed the deadline', because it makes clear who did what.
story:
The cursor blinked in the middle of the unsent email, and Elizabeth read the sentence again. "A delay was experienced with your order, and mistakes were made in the processing." It sounded professional, the way the invoices from the wholesalers sounded, the way the accountant's letters sounded. It also sounded like fog.

She was sixteen and had been handling the shop's email for three weeks, ever since her mother broke her wrist and the cast made typing unbearable. The customer, Mrs. Okafor, had ordered a wreath for her sister's memorial service, and the wreath was nine days late. Nine. Her mother had dictated the apology twice already, and both drafts had died in the drafts folder, too stiff or too raw. Tonight it was Elizabeth's turn, and she had until morning.

She typed a second version. "It has come to our attention that your order was not fulfilled within the promised timeframe." Better, maybe. Worse, possibly. It had a certain smoothness that let everyone slide out from under it, and she noticed, with a small visceral discomfort, how much she liked that smoothness. Nobody was at fault in that sentence. Nobody had done anything at all. She copied it into a message to Martha, who answered within a minute because Martha never slept before one.

Martha's reply was blunt: "id write it like a person not a lawyer." Then a voice note, tinny through the phone speaker, Martha's room sounds behind it. "Okay, so, we covered this in Ms. Friedman's class last month. Plain-language guidance recommends the active voice. That's when the subject does the action. Like 'I missed the deadline.' It makes clear who did what."

Elizabeth typed back "that sounds like confessing to a crime," and Martha typed back "only if you did one," and then a laughing emoji, and then nothing, because Martha's mother called her downstairs.

Elizabeth sat with that. She opened the order history on the shop laptop, half to procrastinate and half because something about the timeline was bothering her, a small splinter of doubt she couldn't locate. Her mother said she'd placed the order on the fourth. Mrs. Okafor's original email was dated the second. Elizabeth scrolled, and the room got quieter around her, the radiator ticking, the smell of the lemon polish her mother used on the counter drifting in from the hall.

There it was. The wreath order sat in the drafts folder of the shop's ordering account, composed on the second, never sent. Whoever had composed it. Elizabeth checked the time stamp and felt her stomach drop, because she remembered the evening: her mother's voice calling from the storeroom, "can you type that in for me, my hand's gone numb," and Elizabeth typing while half watching a video, and then Eleni calling about a party, and the browser tab left open on a screen she never looked at again. The mistake had an author. It was her.

She started a new draft with her hands slightly unsteady on the keys. "Dear Mrs. Okafor, I missed the deadline on your order. I let your wreath sit unsent for a week, and I am sorry." She kept going, saying what had happened and what she would do: the wreath would be hand-delivered tomorrow at no charge, along with the arrangement her mother had already made up as an apology. No sentence allowed anyone to hide. Twice she caught herself drafting a soft escape, a clause like "an error occurred in our system," and twice she deleted it. That was the temptation she hadn't expected, the way passive constructions reached up to exculpate her, quietly, grammatically, while she pretended to be brave.

Still, she couldn't pretend certainty about everything. Whether Mrs. Okafor would forgive it, whether telling the truth would cost her mother a customer, whether honesty was worth more than a wreath for a memorial service that had already happened without it: those were judgments, and she was aware of her thin discernment in such matters, sixteen and three weeks into a job she'd gotten by default. She read the email once more, ears warm, and thought about calling her mother downstairs. Instead she moved the cursor up and pressed send before she could soften anything, and the screen went still, and the drafts folder held only the dead versions, and somewhere across town a notification lit up a phone she could not see.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The hostess stand at Marisol's smelled like lime and burnt tortilla, and Andrew stood beside it holding a clipboard he had not expected to hold. The manager, a man with a pen behind his ear, slid a form across the counter and said, "Fill this out before you clock in tomorrow. It's the I-9."

Andrew looked at the paper. At the top it said Section 1, and beneath that, rows asking who he was and whether he was allowed to work in the United States. He had brought nothing but his phone and a pair of nonslip shoes still in their box. "I don't have, like, a passport on me," he said.

"Section 1 is yours to complete, and it has to be done no later than your first day of paid work." The manager said it flatly, the way he probably said it forty times a summer. "Tomorrow, before your first hour. Not after."

Ryker had gotten him the interview in the first place, had leaned across a lunch table last week and said, my uncle's place, easy money, you in. Andrew had said yes partly because college deposits were due in the fall and partly because Ryker's certainty was the kind that swept people along, and it was easier to be swept than to argue with him. Now, in the booth by the window, Ryker examined the form upside down. "Just sign it tonight and bring whatever tomorrow," he said. "Nobody checks the same day."

"Whoa." Sally set down her agua fresca. She had been hired for the hostess stand and had apparently listened. "You can't clock in without finishing Section 1. Everyone who gets hired here has to do it. It's not a Ryker thing."

Ryker rolled his eyes and said something about bureaucracy existing to subjugate people who just wanted to work, and Andrew let the word pass over him. Six weeks ago he would have let the whole argument pass over him, would have drifted toward whichever voice was louder. His father operated differently, worked from the assumption that rules were suggestions for people who lacked nerve, and for years Andrew had mistaken that confidence for a philosophy. Lately, sitting in English while Ms. Santos-Reyes asked them to weigh one interpretation against another instead of picking the loudest, he had started to notice the difference between a claim and a position, between being certain and having thought something through. The pragmatics of it mattered, he supposed: what a rule actually did, in practice, to actual people, versus what it felt like to complain about.

"I'm not saying it's fair," he said finally. "I'm saying it's a fact about tomorrow." He turned the clipboard over. "If I show up without documents, I don't get paid hours. If I bring my passport, I do. Those are the two versions of the day."

"Look at you," Sally said. "Two-column Andrew."

His mother was at work until eight, but she answered on the second ring, and after some scrapping about where the passport lived, in the fireproof box under the stairs, behind the folder of his grandmother's papers, she agreed to leave it with the neighbor. Andrew biked across town through the heat, the evening sun striking the pavement like something igneous, the streets giving back the day's stored warmth, and the neighbor handed him the blue booklet in a Ziploc bag without asking why, which he appreciated more than he could have said.

The twist came the next morning. He arrived at ten, fifteen minutes early, passport in his shirt pocket, and found the manager apologizing to a girl by the soda station, telling her she couldn't take tables today, telling her to come back when her paperwork was complete. Her Section 1 was unsigned, and her first paid hour was already scheduled. She argued, quietly and then not quietly, and the manager kept saying the same sentence about no later than the first day of paid work, and Andrew stood at the hostess stand with his own blue booklet and felt the argument land somewhere between the two versions of the day he had described to Sally.

He filled out Section 1 at the counter, printed his name, signed, dated it, and set the pen down. Ryker, already aproned and carrying a tray of chips, raised an eyebrow at him from across the dining room. Andrew shrugged, tucked the passport back into his pocket, and followed the manager toward the kitchen. "Table six first," the manager said. "Booth by the window. They always want more salsa than they order."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: The word 'mortgage' comes from Old French for 'dead pledge', because the pledge ends either when the debt is paid or when the property is forfeited.
story:
Parker had the folder of closing documents against his chest when the office door chimed, and he did not put them down, because Mr. Visser had told him never to leave a file where a stranger could read it. The stranger was not a stranger, though. It was Roman, still in his work shirt from the garden centre, rain on his shoulders, holding out his phone.

"Look at this," Roman said.

It was the listing. Two bedrooms above the laundromat on Calder Street, eleven hundred a month, and Parker did the arithmetic before Roman could. First month, last month, and a damage deposit, which the landlord's email said was half a month's rent. Twenty-seven hundred and fifty before they slept a single night there.

"Imran has nine hundred," Roman said. "I've got six."

Which left twelve hundred and fifty, and Parker had four hundred in a savings account he'd been guarding since he was fifteen, and a paycheque from this office that arrived on the fifteenth and was already spoken for by his mother for the phone bill. He did not say any of that. He said, "Give me until Thursday."

Mr. Visser's office ran on Thursdays, closing day, when the buyers came in to sign and Parker carried folders and poured water and stayed out of the way. He had started in June, thinking it would teach him something about houses, and instead it had taught him about money, which turned out to be the same subject. He watched a young couple put eight thousand dollars down on a townhouse, and heard Mr. Visser explain that the down payment was not the price, only the first piece of it, that the rest would be borrowed and paid back for twenty-five years, and that if they stopped paying, the townhouse would stop being theirs. The couple signed anyway. Their pens made a small dry sound.

At the next closing, the lawyer's clerk, an older man who smelled like cough drops, slid the mortgage papers across the table and smiled at them the way people smile at very old jokes. "Mortgage," he said. "Dead pledge. That's the old meaning." Then he tapped the signature line and said nothing more.

Parker carried that home. Dead pledge, he said to Roman that night, over fries at the picnic table behind the garden centre. It means dead pledge, from the old French. The deal ends when the debt is paid off or the place is lost, and until one of those happens the pledge just hangs there, neither alive nor finished. Roman chewed on that longer than he chewed the fries. "So renting is better," he said finally. "Nothing's pledged. You just pay and go."

But Parker had spent the summer watching both kinds of people come through the office, and he could not let it sit that neatly. He was not trying to dichotomize it, rent versus own, safe versus trapped, because the summer had shown him it did not split clean. The couple with the townhouse were paying less each month than the Calder Street apartment cost, and they would own something at the end of it. The man who'd been foreclosed on in July had owned something too, right up until the Tuesday he didn't. What Parker actually wanted, he decided, was not one side of the split. It was a door he could lock from the inside for one year, and he could worry about pledges when he had a paycheque that repeated.

On Wednesday he went through his grandfather's desk looking for the chequebook his mother had asked him to find, and instead found a letter with Parker's own name on it, dated two weeks earlier, never mailed. His grandfather's handwriting had gone shaky but the sentences were still trenchant, each one cut short like it cost him something. Parker, it read. Your mother says you are trying for an apartment and that you are short. I will not hand you a windfall because you would learn nothing from it. But I sold the boat in June, and I have been paying rent on the storage space it used to sit in, which is sixty a month I am no longer spending. I will lend you eight hundred as a loan, repaid at twenty a month starting January, when you will be working at college. Tell me the terms are fair. If they are not, argue. Love, G.

Parker read it three times. He wrote back one line, Terms are fair, except storage was sixty, so make it twenty-five, and mailed it from the box on the corner, and felt the synchronicity of it settle over him quietly: the boat sold, the storage freed, the letter sitting in the desk exactly the summer he needed it, all of it connected and none of it luck in the way Roman would have meant it. It was just money moving, one pile to another, the way it had been moving all summer across the tables at Mr. Visser's.

On Thursday he handed Roman nine hundred in cash, the four hundred savings plus the loan plus what was left of his paycheque after the phone bill, and Roman counted it twice on the picnic table and said, "You're sure." Parker said he was sure, mostly sure, and that mostly was going to have to be enough. Imran texted the landlord from the parking lot, and the three of them stood under the laundromat sign while the reply came through, three words followed by a time on Saturday. Roman read it out loud. "Keys at noon."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Alexandre arrived at the community studio at four, two hours before it closed, and set his sketchbook on the long table between the glaze bins. The youth show opened Friday evening. Tonight was the last firing night for clay, and he had until six to decide whether his panel went into the kiln or stayed home.

The panel was a river seen from above, made of broken tile. He had planned the water as plain gray, a hundred fragments of bathroom tile sorted into a shoebox, because the river in his grandmother's photographs was gray and he wanted to be honest to it. But laid out on the table, the gray looked flat, like pavement, like nothing.

Klara was three seats down, painting at an easel. She kept stepping back from her canvas and frowning at a patch of sky. "This is the same gray in both places," she said to no one, then to Alexandre when he came over with two of his tiles. "Mixed it in one batch. But here it looks warm, almost brown, and here it looks cold, like slate. That's impossible. Paint doesn't change."

"Your light's different," Talha offered from the pottery wheel without looking up. His hands were in a metamorphic lump of clay, gray itself, folding over itself under his palms.

"No, the light's the same. It's the blue next to it. And the orange there." She pointed. "The same gray. It reads two ways."

Alexandre went back to his table. He set one gray fragment on a sheet of blue paper, and another on a sheet he had painted orange, weeks ago, for a sunset he never finished. The fragment on blue looked warm. The fragment on orange looked cool. Same tile, from the same box. He moved them, swapped them, checked the backs for the maker's stamp. Identical.

He found Ms. Sutton at the supply desk and asked if she had anything on color. She dug out a paperback with a cracked spine and said, "Look up Chevreul," and went back to counting brushes. He read at the tall window while Klara painted. The chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. So the gray pushed toward orange warmth against the blue, and toward blue coolness against the orange. Klara's sky had a blue half and a field of orange poppies below it, and her one batch of gray had become two colors without her touching the paint again.

"You were right," he told her. "It's called simultaneous contrast."

"That has a name?"

"Chevreul. 1839. He was a chemist." He held out the book, open to the page, and she read it with a brush in her mouth.

The studio clock said five-forty. Alexandre sat down in front of his river and looked at it differently now. He had been treating the gray as a fixed quantity, a fact about the tile. It wasn't. It was a fact about the tile and its neighbors together. He had spent two years arguing with Talha about exactly this in another form, whether a thing had one nature or only natures-in-relation, though they had never called it that. Talha liked a clean logos, a principle you could state once and apply everywhere. Alexandre had never been able to inure himself to that kind of tidiness, and here, on the table, was his reason laid out in broken bathroom tile. Or it was a reason against his own stubbornness, too. He couldn't tell which. The river wanted to be honest to the photographs. But the photographs had been framed by banks of green, and his tile would be framed by whatever he chose.

He started pulling tiles from the shoebox and laying a border of dull green along the banks. The green made the water go warm where it touched. He had twenty minutes. He worked fast, not gluing yet, only placing, and the gray began to move the way water moves, warmer toward the banks, cooler out in the middle where he set fragments of blue-black slate from the discard bucket. Klara came and stood behind him with her brush still in her hand.

"That's the same gray as before," she said.

"I know."

"Then why does it look like a river now?"

Ms. Sutton called six o'clock from the desk. Alexandre looked at the unglued panel, an hour of drying ahead of it if he started now, the kiln loading at seven with or without him. He picked up the glue.

"It goes in," he said, and turned the first tile over.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
The screen door at her grandmother's house still shrieked on its springs, and Olivia let it bang behind her the way she had every summer since she was six. This August was different. In September she would start at the art program in the city, and the email sitting in her phone said the scholarship applicants needed a portfolio of ten works organized around a single theme, with an artist's statement to hold it together. She had eleven days here, her grandmother's quiet kitchen table, and no theme.

"You've unpacked paints before you unpacked clothes," her grandmother said, setting down a plate of sliced peaches. The juice ran yellow across the white ceramic and smelled like the tree outside the window, the one with the split trunk that had been struck by lightning before Olivia was born.

"Ten pieces," Olivia said. "One idea. All summer I painted whatever I wanted, and now it has to be one thing, and I have to explain it." She tried to verbalize what the theme might be and produced only fragments: doors, hands, her street at dusk, the jars on the shelf above the stove. Her grandmother, who had worked forty years as a seamstress and had a practical sagacity about making things match, said nothing. She slid the peaches closer and went out to water the tomatoes.

That afternoon Olivia sketched the jars, then the tomatoes through the window, then the tree with the split trunk, and hated all three. She texted Yahya, who was building his own portfolio across town. His reply came back in bursts: "they want a statement too." Then: "two actually." Then, before she could ask: "short one for the wall card if you get into the show, like 50 to 100 words. long one for the application, 500 to 1,000. alexis found out the hard way, wrote 300 for the wall and they cut it to ribbons."

Olivia read the message twice. So the words themselves had to come in two sizes, a label and an argument, and she would have to write the argument without yet knowing her own theme. She lay on the hooked rug in the front room, where the afternoon light came through lace curtains and laid a pattern like netting over everything, and listened to the water ticking off the tomatoes outside.

The twist came on Thursday, in the cedar chest under the hall window. She was looking for a blanket and found instead a sketchbook with a cracked spine, her grandmother's name inside the cover in faded pencil, dated the year she emigrated. Olivia sat down on the floor right there and turned the pages. Ten drawings. Only ten: the harbor she had left, the ship's stairwell, the customs hall, a bus bench, the factory window, a row of identical mailboxes, the first kitchen, the seam shop at night, a phone with a long cord, and last, the peach tree, young then, unsplit. Every drawing was of a threshold, a passage, a doorway or window or gate, and Olivia understood that the word for it had been waiting for her in pencil the whole time.

"You drew these," she said that evening, holding the book open to the mailboxes.

Her grandmother looked at the page for a long moment. "I was going to do twenty," she said. "I stopped at ten. Life got profligate with my time, took big handfuls of it." She touched the ship's stairwell with one finger, the nail flattened by decades of pressing seams. "You can use the idea. Ideas are the one thing I have too many of."

Olivia spent the next five days painting doors. The screen door with its shriek. The customs hall drawn from memory and from the sketch, the two of them layered together. She learned that working from her grandmother's drawings meant borrowing a way of seeing, a patience with empty space, and that borrowing it changed her own hand whether she wanted it to or not. The gain was real and so was the cost: her quick, loose brushwork from the spring had to be surrendered, or at least disciplined, and she missed it the way you miss a friend who moves away. Some nights she painted until two and her grandmother sat across the table mending a collar, neither of them speaking, the lamp making one pool of light for both.

On the ninth day she wrote the statements. The long one came out at 600 words, mostly about thresholds and inheritance, and it was honest except for one paragraph she deleted, the paragraph about how strange it felt to build a portfolio on work she hadn't made, on drawings that were better than her own. The short one took her two hours to compress to 80 words, and Alexis texted a photo of her own wall card from a student show, small and square, with the artist's name above the tiny paragraph, proof that the little version had a life of its own on a real wall. Olivia pinned both drafts to the corkboard and stood back.

Her grandmother read the short one at the kitchen table, moving her lips slightly. "You said 'migration' four times," she said.

"Three."

"In the spirit of it, four." She laid the paper down and smoothed it with both hands, the way she smoothed fabric before cutting. She did not say it was good. She said, "You left out the mailboxes."

"The mailboxes are in the long one."

"The mailboxes are the best drawing I ever made." Her grandmother folded her glasses and set them on the peach plate, and outside the split tree stood black against the last of the light, holding up its two halves of crown. Olivia took down the short statement, uncapped her pen, and crossed out her first sentence to make room.
